src.t.12phzb6: PostGrease. The database that remembers everything, if the power stays on. The boss wants it live by Friday.
src.t.831f9a: I pulled the plug, tripped over the cable and typed SELECT with my elbow. It was all still there. I am putting this on my CV.
src.t.96kih1: Rıza’s napkin is more reliable. He is already updating it by hand.
src.t.sckjrr: Sam jumps, the tea sparkles, nothing flickers. Put it in a box and call it a classic.
src.t.2dj4cf: It plays. Mostly. My nephew says the planks are “optional”.
src.t.bwzx5z: Where did the floor go? Why is the sky pink with squares? Is that intentional?
src.t.nxa1gq: I asked for a game. This is a screensaver with ambitions.
src.t.nxg9wo: To read last month’s menu you start from the first and follow the notes. Long chains are tiny and slow to follow, short chains are bigger and quick. The *window* is how many menus you look through to find a good one to compare with.
src.t.3gv9rl: Sixty-four people send a parcel at four o’clock. Three counters open. Everybody waits. A *cache* is like keeping the stamps at the counter: every parcel goes in half the time.
src.t.1aw6qj5: And one test in seven is *flaky*, it fails sometimes for no reason, like my samovar on humid days. With a retry the runner tries again and the good build stays green. Without it someone gets a red cross and writes an angry message.
src.t.pz2ksx: The doorman of a tea house knows three answers: come in, wait here while I ask the owner, or not today. A typo fix with a green check: come in. A 3 a.m. hotfix: wait, call the one who is awake.
src.t.suqawx: Force-pushes, secret keys, a four-hundred-megabyte video of the boss: not today. And “I am the boss” is not a review. The boss is the person who most needs one.
src.t.1ljyfra: Push goes in, objects get stored, merges come out. A rule at the door, a queue at the back. Eight boxes. I have a tunnel to catch.
src.t.erhay2: Four friends, forty branches and one deadline. They push their work here and pull everybody else’s.
src.t.5jta79: A doorman for the main branch. Typo fix with a green check: in. Force-push, a secret key or a 400 MB video: not today.
src.t.n7i73v: Everything is stored under the fingerprint of its content. Same file twice, stored once. Change a byte and the id changes, so damage cannot hide.
src.t.1qyseqa: Old versions of a file are stored as the small difference from another version. The disk bill shrinks; reading gets a few steps longer.
src.t.kul60b: Finds what changed between two versions by keeping the longest run of lines they share. A good diff is short and can be applied.
src.t.x2f9r9: Compares each branch with the common ancestor. What only one side changed goes in; where both changed the same lines, it asks a human.
src.t.1vnzfji: The website: file tree, history graph, diffs and the big merge button. It shows exactly what the boxes above compute.
src.t.kjg1ev: Machines that run the tests on every push. Too few and everyone waits in a queue; too many and the bill grows.
src.t.w71ik7: Demo time. Show me GitHan. And it better not crash.
src.t.1vo9qx2: GitHan. Where code stays the night. Branches, pull requests and a very opinionated merge button.
src.t.dmfgaj: I pressed the green button forty times. Nothing vanished. Ece is crying, but with joy.
src.t.1x532qp: I merged Kaan’s branch and my own commit disappeared. I do not know which of us was deleted.
src.t.1nwm1yy: Computers do many things at once. This is a lie. They do *one* thing, very fast, and hope you do not look. I want the part that decides what.
src.t.12plb8v: It’s called *Linüks*. Like the other one, but with an umlaut. We put it in the kernel. I have heard the kernel is where the popcorn is.
src.t.ddiqh: It must be *completely fair*. Except to my video, which comes first. And my editor. And nobody touches the miner. I mean, the *thing* in the corner. It is mine. It is not mine.
src.t.j66wns: The miner is minerd, pid 4242, nice zero, and it has been eating a third of the CPU since March. We will *renice* it to 19 once the scheduler respects nice.
src.t.18hj8ip: Fair means this: everyone has a ticket clock. The clock runs slower for important people. Whoever is furthest behind gets served. I do this with the tea queue and nobody has complained since 2019.
src.t.180wx1s: There is a maintainer. Gunnar Nakken. I read the list. He once replied to a patch with only the word “no”. Then he replied “no” to that.
src.t.351k6j: Open the 📋 board. The clock, the queue and the lock are three separate jobs. The timeslice needs the first two; the patch and the boot come last.
src.t.b7jzfn: One tea machine, forty thirsty people. The scheduler is the person who decides whose glass is filled next, and for how long, so everyone thinks they are being served at the same time.
src.t.1fwpx91: The turn is short, a few milliseconds. If it is too short I spend all day walking between glasses; too long and the one who only wants a sip waits at the back.
src.t.ho663a: Each guest has a card: how many glasses I have had. I serve whoever has the *least*. That is fair, and it is also what vruntime is: a clock of CPU time received.
src.t.8hcx7w: But the boss pays for *three* glasses to everyone’s one. So his card fills slower: each glass counts for a third. The clock runs at one over the weight. That is what nice does: nice -5 is a weight of about 3000, nice 19 only 15.
src.t.1526vwy: Forget the division and everyone’s card fills at the same speed, and the miner you wanted to hide at nice 19 has as many glasses as the boss.
src.t.1d0uwv2: The cards are kept in a sorted tree, like pigeonholes: the smallest number is always in the leftmost hole, and the kernel keeps a finger on it. Taking the next one costs nothing. Putting a card back costs a few steps down the tree.
src.t.1nx5dzc: The line of people in order of arrival is the wrong tool. And “highest priority always first” is worse: the important ones eat all the tea and the backup waits until Tuesday. Forever.
src.t.eh23pt: Every time I move to another glass I lose a moment: the tray, the spoon, the lemon. In a CPU that is the cache going cold, and it costs about as much as a good chunk of a millisecond.
src.t.r23ar6: So there is a *target latency*, everybody gets a turn within it, and a *minimum granularity*, no turn is shorter than this, however many are waiting. The right numbers are a compromise between a snappy vim and a fast compile.
src.t.gb47j3: A sleeper wakes up with a card that has very few glasses on it, because it slept while others drank. With *wakeup preemption* the kernel notices: “this one is far behind” and serves it right away, instead of letting the compile finish its slice.
src.t.12fxmok: But the kernel itself must let go. With *none* preemption a task in a system call cannot be interrupted at all. *Voluntary* adds polite places to stop. *Full* lets almost anything be interrupted, and costs a little speed. And HZ is how often the metronome ticks.
src.t.1olkgze: Reading the list of all tasks. A spinlock is a door with one key: the others stand outside and ask “is it free yet?” until they are dizzy. A mutex sends them to sleep in the armchair, but some people, like the OOM killer, are not allowed to sit down.
src.t.12hglme: *RCU* is a notice board. Readers just read it, all at once. The writer pins a new notice, waits until everyone who read the old one has gone home, then takes the old one down. Perfect when there are many readers and few writers: our case exactly.
src.t.1p66ze7: It travels by mail, plain text, to the person in charge of that part. Subject with the part’s name in front. Then *why*, because the code already shows the what. Then proof it works. Then your signature that the work is yours.
src.t.hx2cxi: Gunnar Nakken, who looks after the scheduler, answers many patches with one word. It is “NAK”. The trick is to send him nothing he can say it about.
src.t.ho8bw4: A graph is a map made of dots and arrows: the intersections are the dots, the streets are the arrows between them.
src.t.1faqsox: g.add draws one arrow from one intersection to another. A two-way street needs two arrows, a one-way street only one.
src.t.1kqipad: The road file marks one-way streets with this flag: they may be driven from a to b, never back.
src.t.10ahlq2: The length of the street in kilometres. The router turns it into minutes later, when it knows how fast the traffic is.
src.t.1hlrc6s: The guess is A*’s hunch of how long is left to B. Honest hunches keep the answer exact; a hunch that is too big hurries to a worse answer.
src.t.5n1pxs: straightKm is the distance as a crow flies. No road can be shorter than that, which is what makes it a safe base for a guess.
src.t.19it2l7: TOP_SPEED is the fastest any road can be driven. Distance divided by it is the least time any trip could possibly take.
src.t.1uwyevb: A min-heap always hands you the smallest item first. The router keeps its to-do list in one: cheapest-looking intersection next.
src.t.29ktb2: relax asks: is going through this intersection a cheaper way to reach the next one than what I know? If so, remember it.
src.t.5r2loq: Each intersection remembers where it was reached from. pathTo walks that chain backwards from B to A, and that is the route.
src.t.1o8uoul: cost turns a street into minutes: its length over the speed right now. This is where the traffic model plugs in.
src.t.1u4zamh: normalise makes two spellings comparable before they are compared: lower case, and maybe the Turkish letters folded to plain ones.
src.t.1gu6qbq: asciiFold turns ş into s, ı into i, ö into o. People on a phone without a Turkish keyboard type it that way.
src.t.1bo8pwc: MAX_EDITS is how many wrong letters a search may have and still count. Too few and typos fail; too many and Moskova becomes Moda.
src.t.1thwdet: editDistance counts the fewest letters you must add, remove or change to turn one word into the other. Taksm to Taksim is one.
src.t.1pckzbl: With this on, “Kadık” already finds Kadıköy: the words that start with what you typed so far.
src.t.g2lews: When two places are equally close to what you typed, take the one more people go to. Ties are broken by the crowd.
src.t.1y5rsog: prerender is the deepest zoom level drawn in advance. Every level below it is ready before anyone asks; deeper ones wait for a visitor.
src.t.kli0q0: Lazy means draw a tile the first time somebody asks, then keep it. The second visitor gets it instantly.
src.t.13bpgz2: Picture tiles are finished images. Vector tiles are the road lines and the phone draws them: much smaller, a little work for the phone.
src.t.1f9qaog: The route cache keeps the answers to trips people ask again and again. Taksim to Kadıköy is asked a thousand times a minute.
src.t.31q80t: ttl is how many seconds a cached route is kept. Long means more hits but older traffic; short means fresh ETAs and more work.
src.t.6gqy37: The order book is two lists: everyone who wants to buy, best price first, and everyone who wants to sell, best price first.
src.t.1k3q7cf: crosses asks: does the best price on the other side meet this order? A buy at 50.02 crosses a seller at 50.01. A buy at 49.90 does not.
src.t.4y833e: A level is everyone waiting at one price. bestLevel is the queue at the best price on the other side.
src.t.nzi9y8: sortBy puts the queue in the order we will serve it. Whoever is first after sorting is filled first.
src.t.16v0dcq: seq is the order’s arrival number, stamped by the exchange. A smaller seq means you were there first.
src.t.708dya: Pro-rata: split the incoming order between everyone in the queue by how big their orders are. Fair to the big, not to the early.
src.t.aahzb0: rem is what is left of the order to fill. The loop runs until it is zero or nobody on the other side will trade with it.
src.t.tid6s7: takeFrom walks the queue in the order we just chose, trading at each resting order’s own price, until the incoming order is done.
src.t.jcm5o8: Basis points: a hundredth of a percent. 30 of them is 0.30%, charged to whoever takes a price that was waiting.
src.t.1duqmb8: A negative fee is a rebate. Whoever puts a price in the book and waits is paid for it: the exchange needs people who wait.
src.t.bvrgit: bps is the rate in basis points. qty times px is the money that changed hands, in cents; times bps over ten thousand is the fee.
src.t.63chao: 10,000 basis points make one whole. Dividing by it turns a rate in basis points into a fraction.
src.t.19nyxi0: px is the price in whole cents: $50.03 is 5003. No decimals anywhere in the money.
src.t.1k8jdx5: You cannot charge a fraction of a cent. round goes to the nearest cent, floor always goes down. Decide once, on every fill.
src.t.s7zp7a: BAND is how far from the reference price a limit price may be: 0.05 means five percent either way. A zero too many is nine hundred percent.
src.t.1rzvcqk: MAX_QTY is the biggest order we accept. Real funds send twenty thousand shares; a typo sends a hundred and fifty thousand.
src.t.9xy7ev: The reference price is what the market has recently been: the median of the latest orders. The band is measured from it.
src.t.zhyalf: Runs before the order touches the book. Rejecting here costs nothing; letting a silly order trade costs everyone.
src.t.1ey6udr: How big a move is too big: 0.05 means five percent. Too small and the market stops for every piece of news.
src.t.129bhk9: The window is how far back the move is measured: five percent in five minutes is a cliff, five percent in a day is a Tuesday.
src.t.1tzhxpg: How long trading stops. Long enough for people to think and quotes to come back; short enough that the day is not lost.
src.t.1wfo9j6: Shards: the symbols are split between engines, one engine per shard. One symbol can never be split, so the busy one stays on one engine.
src.t.1yip0rn: The journal is the engine’s diary on disk. After a crash it replays the diary and nobody’s order is lost. How often it is written is the question.
src.t.1orfw5p: IDLE_RPM is the speed we want, 850. n_est is the speed the ECU believes in, worked out from the crank sensor. Target minus estimate is the error, and the whole controller is about making it zero.
src.t.1is0bzu: The proportional part: the bigger the error right now, the more the valve moves. Quick, but it needs an error to push, so on its own it never quite gets back to the target.
src.t.1rllo4i: The integral part adds up the error over time, so a small error that lasts still builds up enough push to remove itself. Danger: while the valve is stuck at its end stop it keeps adding up for nothing, and overshoots later. That is called windup.
src.t.pkyu9g: U_BASE is the valve opening that holds idle on a warm engine with nothing switched on. U_AC is the extra opening we already know the A/C compressor will need, so we give it before the revs fall: feed-forward.
src.t.1djeup5: The A/C request, a signal the ECU gets before the compressor clutch closes.
src.t.1sa2m2r: iac_duty is how long the idle air valve is open, in per cent. It has end stops: fully closed and fully open. Asking for more than that changes nothing.
src.t.123ihj2: The time between two runs of this function: the control task period, in seconds.
src.t.1o480n1: The grid lines of the table: the engine speeds down the side, the loads across the top. The table only holds numbers at the crossings.
src.t.1r2rmvy: Finds which square of the grid the point is in: the grid line before it. The next one is index + 1.
src.t.k9m09m: Takes the closest grid crossing and uses its number as is. Cheap, but the answer jumps whenever you cross the halfway line between two crossings.
src.t.ws4bbl: How far between the two grid lines the point is, from 0 to 1. At 0.5 you are in the middle and the answer is the average.
src.t.b73566: Linear interpolation: a slide between two numbers. Do it along the load twice, then once along the speed, and you have a bilinear lookup.
src.t.z35s20: The table’s size. The last row is N_ROWS − 1; one past it is the next thing in memory, which is not a spark angle.
src.t.16rqp10: How long, in milliseconds, a signal has to be bad before the ECU believes it. Crank 40, throttle 200, CAN 40.
src.t.14zpfgd: The debounce counter, one per watched signal. It counts bad time up, and good time down.
src.t.hhjsd6: True if, at this moment, the signal is out of range or does not make sense. A single glitch makes it true once.
src.t.2ert70: Stores the diagnostic trouble code and turns on the reaction: limp-home mode, a lit warning lamp.
src.t.1mnoo5k: Which byte of a 16-bit number goes first on the wire. Big endian (Motorola) sends the high byte first, little endian (Intel) the low one. If the sender and the receiver disagree, 3000 rpm turns into 12 000.
src.t.1uojgp1: How many rpm one bit is worth. The receiver multiplies the raw number by its own value, so the two must be the same number.
src.t.1fwxzh8: Raw bytes cannot be negative. An offset of −40 means raw 0 is −40 °C, so a frozen engine can be reported.
src.t.1o6uaca: How often the frame is sent. A needle that is a second old is no needle.
src.t.175o3zy: End-to-end protection: a counter that goes up in every frame shows lost frames, and a CRC8 over the bytes shows frames damaged on the wire, which the receiver then ignores.
src.t.exwj7k: The period of the control task: injection, spark and idle valve are recomputed this often. A shorter period reacts faster and costs more CPU.
src.t.1l00j5n: The period of the diagnostic task: the sensor checks and fault counters. Faults can be found no faster than this, and the debounce counts in steps of it.
src.t.1rqh5e: Cooperative: a task runs until it is finished, even if a more urgent one is waiting. Preemptive priority: the urgent task cuts in at once, and the interrupted one carries on after.
src.t.j2bjsf: A guard dog in the chip. The control task feeds it every run; if it goes hungry for this long, the dog resets the whole ECU.
src.t.c5sc1w: L1 and L2 are the lengths of the two arm segments: 30 and 25 centimetres. With them and the target, you have a triangle.
src.t.12s4hdc: c2 is the cosine of the elbow angle, from the law of cosines: three sides of a triangle (the two segments and the line to the target) fix its angles.
src.t.wqd5vw: acos turns that cosine back into an angle. A cosine has two angles, plus and minus: elbow up and elbow down. And acos only exists for numbers from −1 to 1.
src.t.3tuair: The number is squeezed into −1 … 1. A target that is too far away then gives a fully stretched arm that points at it, instead of NaN.
src.t.159fctt: atan2 gives the direction of a point as an angle. The shoulder points at the target, minus what the bent elbow takes away.
src.t.1i3swrn: t1 is the shoulder angle and t2 the elbow angle, in radians. Two numbers are all the firmware needs to know where the arm is.
src.t.1nw33ul: kp, the proportional gain: how much current for each radian of error. A stiff spring.
src.t.15z8eot: The integral adds up the error over time, so a small error that stays eventually pushes hard. It is what finally holds the weight of the arm.
src.t.wb1vcy: kd, the derivative gain: a damper. It pushes against the speed, so the arm arrives calmly instead of ringing like a bell.
src.t.1u0vf0p: A low-pass filter smooths a signal. The encoder counts in steps, so its speed jumps between zero and a lot; the filter keeps what is slow and drops the jitter.
src.t.16873ah: The joint speed, from the difference of two encoder readings divided by the time between them. dv is the filtered one.
src.t.1w6th50: The previous encoder reading, kept to compute the speed. It is the measurement, not the error: it does not jump when the setpoint does.
src.t.54ohys: The previous error. The derivative of the error jumps when the setpoint jumps: a derivative kick, a huge push for one tick.
src.t.1h2440q: The anti-windup clamp: the integral may be at most 60% of full current. Without it, the integral keeps filling while the motor is already at its limit.
src.t.1ug989q: dt is the time between two control ticks: a thousandth of a second at 1 kHz. Speeds and sums are all scaled by it.
src.t.oe0maj: The soft limits of each joint, a little inside the hard stops. Past them, the arm is where no arm should be.
src.t.nhwc0j: A fault is anything wrong: the emergency stop is pressed, a joint is past its limit, or a command is not a number.
src.t.lkx75d: The big red mushroom button. Somebody will press it while shouting, and it must work every single time.
src.t.1jm8tli: NaN is “not a number”: the result of a maths mistake, like the arc cosine of 1.2. A motor command that is NaN cannot be trusted.
src.t.2dcurx: Cuts the current to the motors. Alone it lets the arm fall, which is why it comes with the brake.
src.t.174qd7t: The brake clamps the joints without power: a spring pushes it on, and it takes current to open. No power, it holds.
src.t.8l8tkd: Latched: it stays in the fault state after the cause is gone. Somebody must look at the arm and press reset on purpose.
src.t.c2hp02: Limp mode: at most a fifth of the current. A weak arm that is still going somewhere is not stopped.
src.t.1f8skep: All motor commands to zero. No torque, no brake: the arm is as heavy as it was a second ago.
src.t.jppfm4: The shape of speed against time. A jump asks for everything at once; a trapezoid ramps up, cruises and ramps down; an S-curve rounds the corners of the ramps too.
src.t.1jwmbvo: The cruise speed limit of the joint that has the farthest to go. The other joint is slowed to arrive at the same moment.
src.t.4iimry: The acceleration limit. The tea in the glass feels acceleration, not speed: that is what spills it.
src.t.1jj73gb: How many times a second the control loop runs. Faster reacts sooner, but each tick must finish before the next one starts.
src.t.1xqj7bj: Floating-point numbers. This chip has no FPU, so every multiplication is a little program of its own: about eight times slower than Q15.
src.t.547vfn: Q15: whole numbers read as −1 … +1 in steps of 1/32768. Fast, but when a sum goes past +1 it wraps around to −1: full forward becomes full backward.
src.t.5n1pha: Q15 that saturates: a sum past +1 stays at +1. A tiny bit slower and it never flips the sign.
src.t.tn40zs: The cut-off of the derivative filter. Low: calm but slow. High: quick, and it passes the jitter of the encoder’s steps.
src.t.18rmdy0: The watchdog resets the chip if the loop has not checked in for this many milliseconds. Too long and a frozen arm runs on; shorter than one loop period and it resets a healthy chip.
src.t.wvtees: The most current the driver may push into the motors. Holding the glass at full stretch needs about 6 A; a jam at much more cooks the driver.
src.t.scj1sb: The wheelbase is the distance between the two wheels, 25 cm. A turn is how much further one wheel rolled than the other, measured against that distance.
src.t.1mf1xxh: The gyro is a tiny chip that feels rotation itself. It does not care whether the wheels slip, and it drifts only a little over a long day.
src.t.b4nbzm: dth is the change of heading: how many radians the robot turned in this one step.
src.t.1mg4ftz: dl and dr are how far the left and the right wheel rolled in this step, counted by the encoders on the axles.
src.t.dqvkua: The pose is where the robot thinks it is: x, y, and which way it faces, th.
src.t.p1mo3a: integrate adds this step’s little bit to what is already known, again and again all day. Dead reckoning has no way to look outside, so a small mistake is never forgotten.
src.t.6loaey: L_OCC is the evidence one beam adds to the tile it ends on. Log-odds: every hit nudges the tile a little towards “wall”.
src.t.4ujof7: L_FREE is the evidence for “air” from a beam that flew over a tile. It is negative, and weaker than a hit, because flying over is weaker proof than hitting.
src.t.1kp346b: The grid is the map: one number per 30 cm tile. Above zero means wall, below zero means air, zero means nobody has looked.
src.t.pt7z16: air is every tile between the robot and the place the beam ended. The beam got through, so those tiles are empty.
src.t.tbmory: A scan is one turn of the lidar: a ring of beams. Each beam says how far it flew, and whether it hit something or ran out of range.
src.t.1o451t6: These work out which tiles a beam passed over, from the robot’s pose and the beam’s angle. A straight line through a grid.
src.t.hbw4x5: DARK is the brightness below which a pixel counts as “something dark”. Pixels run from 0, black, to 1, white.
src.t.1ld48x6: Sobel slides a 3 by 3 window over the picture and measures how fast the brightness changes. A flat floor gives nothing, the edge of a cable gives a lot.
src.t.q3a7yx: img is the camera’s picture: 144 numbers, a 12 by 12 grey square, 0 for black and 1 for white.
src.t.4kx1lj: full saves a copy of the whole photo for every step of undo. A 24-megapixel copy is 96 megabytes.
src.t.jmh5d7: tiles saves only the tiles a stroke changed. A brush stroke touches a handful of them.
src.t.1uvihxn: A tile as wide as the photo itself: no tiling at all, and every change copies everything.
src.t.1n8pkku: lerp is a step a fraction t of the way from one point to another: nought stays, one arrives, a half is the middle.
src.t.25s5tz: A cubic Bézier: four points. The first and last are on the curve, the middle two are handles that pull it without touching it.
src.t.1gfyyp3: ab, bc and cd are the first round of lerps: a point on each side of the control polygon, all at the same fraction t.
src.t.h2zerx: t runs from nought at the start of the curve to one at its end. It is time along the curve, not distance.
src.t.1y0u123: Paul de Casteljau worked this out for Citroën in 1959: mix pairs, then pairs of pairs, until one point is left. It was a company secret for years.
src.t.rkc5ks: tol, the tolerance: the most a segment may stray from the true curve, in screen pixels. A quarter of a pixel is invisible.
src.t.191dsyv: subdivide cuts the curve at its middle and asks each half the same question, again and again, until the piece is straight enough.
src.t.vwp44i: The chord is the straight line between a piece’s two ends. The less the curve bulges away from it, the straighter the piece.
src.t.1a9q5pi: pointAt asks the Bézier code for the point at a given t. Flattening is built on it.
src.t.1bfsgea: rayCast shoots a ray from the click to the right and looks at every edge of the shape it crosses.
src.t.pviirc: wn, the winding number: edges crossed going up count plus one, going down minus one. How often the outline circles the point.
src.t.4kjxw6: cross counts how many edges the ray crossed, whichever way they went.
src.t.1ay77pd: Even-odd: inside if the ray crosses an odd number of edges. Two circles in the same direction make a ring, because the middle is crossed twice.
src.t.urd0v: The bounding box is the smallest upright rectangle around the shape. Quick to check, and it knows nothing about holes.
src.t.mribww: The fill rule is part of the shape: non-zero or even-odd. It decides which regions of a self-crossing or nested outline are painted.
src.t.1x9dty5: JOIN is what happens at a corner of a thick line: the outer edges can meet in a point, a curve or a cut-off.
src.t.ol6l3t: Miter: the outer edges are extended until they meet, in a sharp point. The sharper the corner, the longer the point.
src.t.1s7s8i9: Round: a circular arc around the corner’s point, or a half-circle at the end of a line.
src.t.1eyecj8: Bevel: the corner is cut off flat, like a chamfered table.
src.t.6ryv96: CAP is what the two ends of an open line look like: flat at the end point, rounded, or squared past it.
src.t.1ojfo22: Butt: the line stops exactly at its end point, flat across.
src.t.16ekhls: Square: the line sticks out half its width beyond the end point.
src.t.1jq1hjt: MITER_LIMIT: if a miter’s point would be longer than this many half-widths, the join is bevelled instead. It is what stops a sharp corner growing a spike.
src.t.11fbl9n: AA, anti-aliasing: how many samples inside each pixel decide its shade. One sample gives staircases; more give smooth edges.
src.t.1xe5ev5: Samples per pixel row: 4 or 16 scanlines, with the horizontal coverage worked out exactly. Cost grows with the number.
src.t.16ioyi1: TOLERANCE is the flattening tolerance, the most the polygon may stray from the curve.
src.t.14u1gso: UNITS says what the tolerance is measured in: screen pixels follow the zoom, document units do not, and zoomed in they become large polygons.
src.t.1a4fdf5: In screen pixels: the tolerance is divided by the zoom, so a zoomed-in curve is cut into more pieces.
src.t.1c4aq6u: In document units: the same size on the page whatever the zoom, so zoomed in it is huge on the screen.
src.t.1akuxo2: The timecode label: hours, minutes, seconds and a frame, like 00:01:00;02. A semicolon before the frames means drop-frame.
src.t.9ysnvc: The label counts 30 frames to every “second”, though the camera makes 29.97. Nominal is that round number on the label, not the real speed.
src.t.1da0igv: Every frame if each labelled second really had 30. Right on a 30 fps camera; on ours it runs ahead of the clock.
src.t.9e0j84: Whole minutes on the label. Drop-frame needs them: it skips two labels at the start of each minute, except every tenth.
src.t.rd1q5i: The camera’s true speed as a fraction: 30000 frames in every 1001 ticks of a second. That is 29.97, not 30.
src.t.8w69pk: One pixel’s brightness in linear light: double the number, double the light. The right numbers to mix and add, but not what a screen shows.
src.t.2p1agr: A LUT, look-up table: the colourist’s look as a table. Give it a value as seen on a screen and it hands back the graded one.
src.t.1dsfq15: Squeezes linear light with the sRGB curve, the way screens expect: dark tones get more of the numbers, because eyes fuss over darks.
src.t.l0l505: features is what the classifier gets to see instead of the picture. Choose what it sees and you choose what it can learn.
src.t.8bmb1v: beams: how many distances the lidar measures per turn. More beams catch thin chair legs, and each one costs the chip time.
src.t.xrh2tj: The lidar’s reach in metres. The garage is twelve metres wide: with a short reach, one wall looks much like another.
src.t.1x162qu: Particles are guesses of where the robot is. More guesses find the right place more surely, but the chip scores every guess against every beam.
src.t.zb9kze: How far apart the guesses are spread at every step, to cover the wheels slipping. Too little and the truth falls between the guesses; too much and they scatter.
src.t.1jqi9vv: Resampling copies the good guesses and drops the bad ones. Never doing it leaves a cloud full of hopeless guesses; doing it too eagerly loses variety.
src.t.1ytwx79: When on, a robot whose scan stops fitting the map searches the whole map for a better match. Off, and a robot that was picked up stays lost for ever.
src.t.1q5o48n: The pattern is the order the robot visits the floor in: bouncing about at random, in a spiral, or in straight lanes like mowing a lawn.
src.t.1nz1das: Lane spacing is how many tiles lie between two lanes. The brush reaches a little beside the robot, but not far.
src.t.1m2jbb1: Suction is how hard it pulls. Carpet holds its dirt deep: tiles come clean on eco, carpet does not. And strong suction drains the battery.
src.t.1narzsp: The battery level, in percent, at which the robot stops cleaning and goes to the dock. The dock is a long way from the far corner.
src.t.17py7bh: The cliff sensor looks down. If its reading falls below this number the floor is too far away, so it is a drop, and the robot stops.
src.t.6wba46: decode turns a stored number back into an amount of light. The numbers in a photo are squeezed so dark tones get more of them: 0.5 is only a fifth of the light of 1.
src.t.1a6pput: encode is the way back: from an amount of light to the number the file and the screen expect.
src.t.lr1r36: mix puts the layer over what is below, by alpha, after running the blend mode: multiply, screen or overlay.
src.t.1nzjrsi: The blend mode: multiply darkens, screen lightens, overlay does both around the middle. Normal just covers.
src.t.1emelm5: Alpha is how opaque a pixel is: one is solid, nought is not there. A soft edge has values in between.
src.t.1nt1scx: The kernel is a row of weights that add up to one. Each new pixel is the old pixel and its neighbours, added up with these weights; a Gaussian makes them a bell.
src.t.135pngu: Premultiplying scales the colour by its alpha first, so a see-through pixel counts for nothing. Unpremultiply divides it back out afterwards.
src.t.1wbjavw: One pass of the kernel along every row, or every column. A Gaussian can be done as the two, one after the other.
src.t.yjm5ql: One big square kernel, made by multiplying the row of weights by itself. It gives the same answer, with far more multiplications.
src.t.10m9bbp: surround collects the ring of pixels just outside the hole: what the hole’s edge should join up with.
src.t.1u1hvu4: The ring is the border of good pixels around the scratch, three pixels deep. A good fill continues it without a seam.
src.t.13ottqc: bestPatch tries every nearby spot and keeps the one whose own ring is most like this ring, by summed squared difference.
src.t.1emrxfv: paste copies the pixels from inside the winning patch into the hole.
src.t.15j6u5i: The mean colour: add them all up and divide. Fine for a clear sky, a smear for a brick wall.
src.t.135j1iu: stretch repeats the column of pixels just left of the hole all the way across.
src.t.96g8fq: EDGE says what a filter sees beyond the photo’s border, where no pixels exist: it has to make some up.
src.t.1eipht: clamp repeats the outermost pixel as far as needed. Quiet and safe.
src.t.1kj99g8: mirror reflects the photo at its border, as if a mirror stood there.
src.t.k6174g: wrap brings in the opposite side of the photo, as if it were printed on a cylinder. The left edge bleeds into the right.
src.t.1joghgh: zero treats everything beyond the border as black. The blur drags that black in, and the picture gets a dark frame.
src.t.177ccul: RADIUS is how far the unsharp mask looks around each pixel to find what is “blurry”: a few pixels for fine detail, many for broad contrast.
src.t.wpjfs6: AMOUNT is how much of the detail the mask adds back. One is the detail again; four is a drawing in thick pencil.
src.t.oxbocg: THRESHOLD ignores differences smaller than this, out of 255, so grain and sensor noise are not sharpened along with the edges.
src.t.4idc6z: The unsharp mask subtracts a blurred copy from the photo and adds the difference back. Edges get stronger; the name comes from the darkroom.
src.t.qo33rm: What undo remembers per step: the whole picture, or just the tiles the stroke touched.
src.t.m56hep: How many steps of undo are kept. More is kinder to the retoucher and harder on the memory.
src.t.19l5aaq: The photo is cut into square tiles of this many pixels. Drawing, undo and the cache all work one tile at a time.
src.t.1cvpteo: Decoded tiles kept in memory, in megabytes. Panning back to a place you just saw costs nothing if its tiles are still here.
src.t.1bcmi6i: Samples of sound per second in the project. The camera recorded 48000; at any other rate the sound has to be converted.
src.t.k5qqlh: How sound is converted to another rate. “none” plays the samples as they are, only slower or faster. The others compute new samples in between.
src.t.129i8y7: Draws a straight line between two samples and reads the new sample off it. Quick, but it rounds off the highest notes and adds a hiss.
src.t.18jjvwc: Rebuilds the sound wave between samples from many neighbours, with the sinc function. Slower, and almost exact.
src.t.1txkg9p: How many samples of sound sit under each picture. At 48000 and 29.97 it is 1601.6: never a whole number.
src.t.ucrc1z: floor and ceil round every frame the same way, so the leftover tenths pile up. cycle keeps the leftover and hands it out: 1602, 1601, 1602, 1601, 1602.
src.t.1yvalv0: The sound that plays while picture frame n is on screen. Ask for frame 50,000 and every rounding error before it is in the answer.
src.t.16o89nh: Dominance: how much greener a pixel is than its red and blue. A green screen has plenty; a boss has little, unless the screen’s light falls on him.
src.t.ipbasm: Below this dominance a pixel is boss and stays. Too low and the shadowy parts of his suit start to vanish; too high and the screen’s dark corners stay.
src.t.1pi8p7i: At this dominance a pixel is fully screen and gone. Between LO and HI it fades: that fade is how hair and soft edges survive.
src.t.12tz3dg: Alpha: how much of the pixel is kept. One is solid boss, zero is see-through, and the beach shows behind.
src.t.1cn7upu: Spill: the screen’s green light bounces onto the boss. Despill pulls the green back down on the pixels that stay, so he has no green halo.
src.t.484g6b: What happens where two shots meet. A cut is instant, a dissolve melts one into the other, a dip goes through black.
src.t.1c0egxw: Which numbers the mix is done in. Screen numbers are squeezed, so the middle of the fade comes out dark. Light mixes properly.
src.t.1yrtjxd: How long the mix lasts. It is centred on the cut, so a shot lends its first and last frames to the neighbours.
src.t.2zxqa7: The curve of the mix: how fast it goes at each moment. Linear is one speed all the way; easing starts and stops gently, like a good lift.
src.t.akwavj: Which files the viewer plays: the camera’s 4K originals, or smaller proxies made just for editing.
src.t.1sbl92j: Frames kept decoded in memory. Scrub back over them and they come for free. Too many and the machine runs out of RAM and swaps.
src.t.1xvktje: How big the viewer draws the picture. Half the width is a quarter of the pixels to grade, key and mix every frame.
src.t.1do2i29: Originals have a keyframe every few seconds and frames that lean on each other. h264 proxies are smaller. Intra proxies make every frame a keyframe: biggest files, instant scrubbing.
src.t.1g9o31y: thr is the throttle all four motors share, like four people pushing a shopping cart together. The three commands make some push harder and some softer.
src.t.1qr9r0: Roll tips the drone sideways, pitch tips its nose up or down, yaw turns it on the spot. Think of a tea tray: tilt it left, tilt it forward, spin it.
src.t.85gseh: Props spinning one way push the body the other way round. Two spin clockwise and two counter-clockwise, so the pushes cancel and the drone does not spin. To turn it, speed up one pair.
src.t.jnnv1y: roll is our guess of how far the drone is tipped sideways, in radians. 0 is level.
src.t.ntub6k: The gyro measures how fast the drone turns. Add the turning up over time and you have the angle, but its tiny constant error, the bias, adds up too.
src.t.5obigy: The accelerometer feels which way gravity pulls; atan2f turns the sideways and downward readings into an angle. Right when the drone is still, fooled when it accelerates, like tea slopping when the bus brakes.
src.t.1wsasj4: dt is the time between two readings: 0.002 s, five hundred times a second.
src.t.ufby5i: Bias is a small constant error: a gyro that says the drone is turning a little even when it sits still. Every second adds a bit more.
src.t.1nxgfco: ALPHA is how much of the old angle the filter keeps each step. Near 1 it believes the gyro and lets the accelerometer correct it slowly; low, it follows the accelerometer, noise and fooling included.
src.t.imio42: A Kalman filter keeps a guess and how unsure it is. It trusts whichever sensor has been more reliable lately, and it learns the gyro’s bias on the way.
src.t.1lu1ymh: A low-pass filter lets slow changes through and smooths away fast jitter, like a thick window muffling the street. The cutoff in Hz is where it starts muffling: lower is smoother, but later.
src.t.b6z1dp: A notch filter removes one narrow band of frequencies, here the motors’ 125 Hz hum, and leaves the rest alone. Like muting only the fridge’s buzz.
src.t.14vtu3k: The rate loop’s P: push the motors in proportion to how far the turn rate is from what was asked. Like steering harder the further you are from the lane.
src.t.16pt50r: D reacts to how quickly the turn rate is changing. It damps ringing, but it also amplifies noise, and noisy commands make the motors hot.
src.t.1y6e22w: The angle loop’s P: how fast a turn to ask for, per radian of angle error. Too low is sluggish, too high overshoots.
src.t.rpkx4l: The ESC is the little box that spins each motor. PWM sends a new speed only 50 times a second, OneShot a few hundred, DShot thousands of digital messages with error checking. Late commands make the loops ring.
src.t.xacudy: When one motor hits its limit, airmode slides all four together so the differences between them, the steering, survive. Without it a clipped motor loses its share of the steering.
src.t.1napr0t: The I term adds up small steady errors. On a tilted pad it keeps adding up for as long as the drone sits there, then dumps it all on take-off: integrator windup.
src.t.13lumwm: The gimbal servos turn the camera against the drone’s tilt, like keeping a cup level while you walk.
src.t.eqz7tp: The flight controller’s own estimate of how far the drone is tilted. It is known before the camera has moved, so the gimbal can move first: feed-forward.
src.t.1ripxxn: Between grid points the ECU must slide, not jump; and past the table’s end it must hold the last value, not read the next thing in memory.
src.t.1bvfj23: Every important signal is checked: is it in range, does it agree with the others? A bad reading is counted; only a lasting one becomes a fault code and sends the engine to limp-home.
src.t.yeqxk4: Too eager and a glitch on the wire cripples a healthy car. Too slow and the runaway has already happened.
src.t.1qzlxv3: The car’s office gossip: the ECU shouts engine speed and temperature, the gearbox shouts its torque request. Each frame is eight bytes, packed to a document both sides signed.
src.t.b03cu9: Byte order, scaling and offset must match bit for bit, or the needle shows 12 000 rpm in the garage.
src.t.aaisq0: The engine bolted to a big brake in a cell, with an automation that runs a sequence: warm up, then a grid of speeds and loads, each held until the readings settle. Torque, fuel flow, exhaust temperature, emissions.
src.t.xmnmmk: The numbers it writes become the maps. A short dwell on a cold engine writes noise into the car.
src.t.1my1uao: The real ECU, wired to a computer that plays engine and car. Test cases break wires on purpose and check the reaction. Each requirement has its test: that is the V-model.
src.t.1ob8wg8: Only when the report is green is the image flashed, and then its checksum is read back. No match, no release.
src.t.vncs4a: Demo time. Show me Motorin. And it better not crash.
src.t.1mcgisu: Motorin. The little box that decides how much petrol goes in, and when to light it. Tested on the bench, because the road is not forgiving.
src.t.15sozr: I turned the key on the bench, revved it, pulled a wire and it said P-zero-three-three-five in a dignified tone. Then it kept driving. Like me after a board meeting.
src.t.yt6zgi: It bucked, it stalled, and when I pulled a wire it ignored me. The engineers laughed. I laughed too. Then I stopped.
src.t.1hn28ai: Listen. Investors. Friday. They will not come for the code. They will come for the *tea*, and the tea will be brought by a *robot*.
src.t.eibpc3: It’s called *Çaycı-3000*. A robot arm. It takes the glass from the counter, puts it on the saucer, and does not spill. The competition spills. I have seen the videos.
src.t.v4jg89: Also it should wave at me. And have *AI*. And be *cloud-native*. The arm is in the garage. It is quite heavy. Please do not drop it on Rıza.
src.t.fdjj8o: Tea in a tulip glass sloshes four times a second. If you move the glass like a hammer, it spills on the first swing. Move it like I move it: gently at the start, gently at the end.
src.t.rbq7lp: The arm has a microcontroller with no floating point. I did the maths: a single multiplication takes more than my morning.
src.t.1vk560b: And a red emergency button. Somebody will press it. I would like it to *work*.
src.t.1o6tzak: Open the 📋 board. Inverse kinematics, the PID loop and the safety layer can be done at the same time. Then the motion, the microcontroller and the tuning, and finally flashing the arm.
src.t.wpi6o4: Two sticks joined at the elbow, one end fixed. You want the far end on the glass. It is a triangle: two sides you know, the third is the distance to the glass. Three sides decide the angles.
src.t.heobe7: But a triangle can bend up or down: two arms, same glass. Take the one with the elbow up, or the arm sits in the counter. And if the glass is farther than both sticks together there is no triangle: do not let a square root of a negative number move the arm.
src.t.1yrz5jh: P is me pouring faster the emptier the glass is. D is me watching how fast it fills and slowing down before the top, so it does not run over. I is my memory: “I have been a little short for a minute now, pour more”.
src.t.k49i03: The heavy arm pulls down all the time. With only P, the arm sags until the push equals the weight: it never quite arrives. I fills a bucket until the push is exactly the weight.
src.t.whdl5: The motor is already at its limit but the glass is still far away, and the I bucket keeps filling with “still not there, still not there”. When the arm finally arrives the bucket is full of old complaints, and it overshoots until they drain.
src.t.vbknl2: So: stop filling when the motor can give no more, or put a ceiling on the bucket. And look at the speed, not the error, for D: a new setpoint is a jump in the error and the D term would kick the motor for one tick.
src.t.10bqahu: Tea sloshes like a swing, about four times a second. Accelerate hard and the tea climbs the wall of the glass and goes over. Speed does not hurt it. Changing speed does.
src.t.znul5k: A trapezoid ramps the speed: constant acceleration. An S-curve rounds the corners of the ramp, so even the acceleration changes gently. Slower to start, calmer in the glass. I walk the tray that way.
src.t.1quwmmy: This chip has no floating-point unit. Every decimal multiplication is a little program. A thousand ticks a second of those and the chip is out of breath. Integers in Q15 are ten times quicker, but they live between −1 and +1.
src.t.1tpoyyd: Go past +1 and it wraps to −1: full speed forward becomes full speed backward. Use the saturating kind. And if a tick is not finished when the next one is due, it is simply missed, and the motors keep the last answer.
src.t.13rxp2e: The encoder counts in steps, like a clock with only an hour hand. Speed is the change between two readings, so mostly nothing, and sometimes one whole step in one millisecond. A spike. The D term turns the spikes into a buzz.
src.t.7nkzvz: A low-pass filter averages the last few. Too gentle and the buzz stays; too strong and the answer arrives late, and the damper damps yesterday.
src.t.mycrmo: It is a timer that wants to be fed. Every tick the loop feeds it. If the chip freezes, nobody feeds it and it bites: resets the chip, motors off, brake on.
src.t.knmh85: Too long a timeout and a frozen arm swings across the garage while it counts. Shorter than one tick and it bites a healthy chip at every tick. Slightly more than a few ticks is right.
src.t.qe3guf: An order in, two angles out, a thousand times a second. Everything in the box runs on a chip with no FPU. The safety is the box around the box. I have a call.
src.t.utajhz: The order comes in as a point in space: “the glass is here, the saucer is there.” Nobody orders in joint angles.
src.t.1brut83: Turns a point in space into two joint angles. There are two ways to reach it, elbow up or down, and for a point too far away there is no way at all.
src.t.jp3nz0: Decides how the setpoint travels between two angles. Jump there, ease there, or ease the easing. The tea cares about the last one.
src.t.1pgvezh: One control loop per joint: how far off am I, how long have I been off, how fast am I moving. Stiff but calm, and it must hold the arm against gravity.
src.t.1gqfz67: A small chip that runs everything above on a clock. Its limit is time: if one tick takes longer than the period, ticks are missed.
src.t.1uwafng: Demo time. Show me Mapsiz. And it better not crash.
src.t.21zbcd: Mapsiz. Maps, but you only get lost on purpose. The boss wants to cross the Bosphorus by Friday.
src.t.dp45ay: I drove to Kadıköy by the ferry. It was on the map. Make the ferry louder.
src.t.gqpft2: It sent my driver down a one-way street the wrong way. He is now a one-way person.
src.t.l1wab3: A stock exchange. Everyone has one. Ours will list *our own* products, so the share price is whatever I say it is.
src.t.7z1h4d: It is called *Nasdoq*. Legal says it is a different word. Legal also says it is a different number of letters.
src.t.1pq4rnl: People send orders. We match them. If something goes wrong, we stop the market. I want a button for that. A big red one.
src.t.1dtvexm: Tea, anyone? Three things go wrong on a real exchange: somebody types a zero too many, a fund sells at once into a thin book, and the money does not add up to the cent.
src.t.1ullznn: I will take the money part. I read that floating point is fine. It is probably fine.
src.t.19amuys: Open the 📋 board on a laptop. The engine, the money and the circuit breaker can all start right now.
src.t.1q6uq7j: Two lists, like the queue at my tea counter, but with prices. On top, the people who want to *sell*, cheapest first. Below, the people who want to *buy*, highest first. The gap in the middle is the spread.
src.t.7rr1vc: At every price there is a little queue. A trade happens when the best buyer and the best seller agree. Until then everybody waits, and I serve tea.
src.t.1gsv0aq: Imagine I serve tea to whoever shouts last. Nobody queues, everybody shouts at the end, and the first person goes home with nothing.
src.t.zu6neq: Price-time priority: best price first, and at the same price, whoever came first. Some markets share fills by size, *pro-rata*, which is fine for futures, but then the winner is whoever sent the biggest order, not the earliest one.
src.t.1kp1g9u: A *market* order says “buy now, any price the book has”. A *limit* order says “only at this price or better”, and if nobody agrees, it waits in the queue.
src.t.1lf7ivt: A market order pays the spread for speed. A limit order earns the spread for patience. The exchange pays the patient ones a small rebate, because without them there is nothing to buy.
src.t.1sd7fke: A computer counts in twos, not tens. It cannot write a tenth exactly, the same way I cannot write a third in decimals: nought point three three three…
src.t.19ndcwu: So money is *whole cents*, as integers. Round once, per fill, the same way every time. A thousand fills later, the books and the statements agree to the cent, and the auditors go home early.
src.t.13lpreb: When the price falls too fast, it stops the market for a few minutes. Not to be kind: to let the quotes come back. In a crash the market makers pull their prices, the book empties, and the next seller falls straight through to the floor.
src.t.1kxzgei: Too eager, and every piece of news freezes the market. Too lazy, and the crash is over before it trips. Five percent in five minutes is a common answer.
src.t.1o9el9d: Somebody types 500.00 instead of 50.00. Without a check, the order buys everything for sale at any price, and somebody else is delighted.
src.t.1yyc52r: The pre-trade check is the bouncer: a price band around the recent price, and a maximum size. Set it too tight and it throws out the fund that really wants twenty thousand shares.
src.t.jdm0eb: In the crash a message arrives every forty microseconds. If you send each one in its own envelope, a hundred subscribers get a hundred envelopes each, and the post office falls over.
src.t.qjdu7l: Wait a few milliseconds, send one envelope with the latest prices. A few milliseconds late is better than a hundred times too many.
src.t.8cbux1: The journal is the diary of every order, so a crash can replay it and nothing is lost. Writing in the diary after *every* order means waiting for the disk each time.
src.t.1qfkflo: Write it every few milliseconds instead and you can risk a few milliseconds of orders. Never write it, and a crash forgets the lot. Also, one busy symbol cannot be split between engines. That is why “just add servers” is a lie.
src.t.ksv8b: Orders in, trades out, nobody’s money lost. Nine boxes. The middle one must never be wrong. I have a call.
src.t.1h1m6o4: Market makers who quote both sides, everyday traders, big funds, and now and then somebody with an extra zero on the keyboard.
src.t.127mfyp: The bouncer at the door: a price ten times the market, or a hundred and fifty thousand shares by mistake, never reaches the book.
src.t.yydp5u: When a buy meets a sell the engine trades them. At equal prices, the order that arrived first goes first. That is the promise of a fair market.
src.t.1ywnnj4: Two sorted lists with a queue at every price. The gap between the best buy and the best sell is the spread.
src.t.osi5f4: Every fill pays or receives a fee. Money is counted in whole cents, as integers, rounded once. The auditors do not accept “nearly”.
src.t.kqpph5: Watches the trades. If the price falls off a cliff it stops everything for a few minutes, so people and quotes can come back.
src.t.ml4hzx: Every trade and book change goes out to a hundred subscribers. Batch a few milliseconds and the burst becomes a trickle.
src.t.gyzqi: The engine writes a diary of every order to disk so a crash loses nothing. Writing it for every order is slow, writing it never is quick and dangerous.
src.t.uyq7y6: Demo time. Show me Nasdoq. And it better not crash.
src.t.17wwewy: Nasdoq. The stock market, but only for stocks that are ours. Open at nine, crash at two, apologise at three.
src.t.ju2v83: The red button worked. I pressed it eleven times, just to see. Make it redder.
src.t.slo7op: My shares went to nought point nought nought one in four minutes. A man called Murat bought all of them. Murat, come back.
src.t.1hbgg0q: Gentlemen. Cars. Everybody has one, nobody understands them. Anadolu Motor needs the *brain* for their new Çaycı 1.0. A small box. It has more wires than my last relationship.
src.t.11zz0ok: A small, boring piece of code that watches everything else and can say no. It does not try to be clever; it has to be right.
src.t.1idmrpq: Current in, torque out. Too little current and the arm cannot lift the glass; too much and a jam burns the driver.
src.t.7vylla: The real thing: segments, weight, friction. Picking up the glass changes how heavy the arm is in the middle of a move.
src.t.w985f3: They count the joint angle in steps. Speed is the difference of two counts, which is noisy; and if the zero is wrong, every angle is wrong by the same amount.
src.t.1wa1gll: A timer the loop has to pet every tick. If it forgets, because the chip froze, the watchdog resets everything and the arm stops.
src.t.ewebi1: Demo time. Show me Çaycı-3000. And it better not crash.
src.t.vuv9ln: Çaycı-3000. A robot arm that serves tea without spilling it. The boss wants a demo for the investors on Friday.
src.t.14qokyt: The robot waved at me. Then it served the tea. I did not know it could do both. Put “AI” on the invoice.
src.t.ubk55p: Rıza is in the corner with a towel. The robot is waving at the ceiling. Nobody knows why.
src.t.1s2hnwa: Listen up. Robots. Everyone has a robot. A robot that *cleans*. The garage is a disgrace and I am not touching a broom. I have a reputation.
src.t.84q6e0: It is called *Rumbay*. It must clean by itself, not hit the desks, not eat my phone charger and not fall down the stairs. The stairs are where my last intern went.
src.t.keabad: It needs a map. A map made of *lidar*. I do not know what that is. It has a laser in it and I like it already.
src.t.zitcdg: Tea first. Three things to know. The wheels lie, so the robot must keep checking where it is against its own map. The camera sees what the laser cannot: socks. And a carpet with a pattern is *not* a cable.
src.t.14qhyy2: Last time somebody picked the robot up and put it down in the kitchen. It still thinks it is in the kitchen.
src.t.c6w1by: I can label the photos. Someone do the code and the bench?
src.t.1sm04w6: Because wheels lie. On the tiles they grip, on the carpet they spin. Counting turns is like counting my steps in socks on a wet floor: I took ten, I moved six.
src.t.ehr2z5: And the little mistakes never cancel, they add. After a lap of the garage it believes it is in the kitchen. A *gyro* feels the turning itself, so heading is right. Distance still drifts a little, and that is the map’s job to fix.
src.t.106juza: Every beam of the laser says two things: “all the way along here it was empty”, and “and then something was in the way”. For every tile, it keeps a score. Air pushes it down a little, a hit pushes it up a little.
src.t.126oskv: That is *log-odds*. One bad beam moves a tile a bit, never from wall to air. And when the cat gets up and leaves, the beams that now pass through the cushion slowly wash it out. If you just overwrite the map every turn, the chair legs blink like a bad light bulb.
src.t.1vmn38w: Imagine a hundred of us in the tea garden, each swearing we know where the robot is. Everyone says a different place. Then the laser reads the walls, and we check: if the robot were *there*, would the walls look like this?
src.t.4knvwr: Whoever fits keeps their place and gets copied, the others go home. Next step, everyone moves a bit with the wheels, and we do it again. After a few turns all of us stand in the same spot. If you have too few of us, nobody happens to stand in the right place and it is lost for good. If the robot is picked up, you send everyone out across the whole map and see who fits.
src.t.yrdl21: The camera gives a tiny grey picture. A fixed “dark means junk” rule misses the white charger and fires on every dark stripe of the carpet. Better to look at where the picture *changes*: that is a Sobel filter. A cable has sharp edges in any light.
src.t.1wl6oq9: Then a small network learns what a cable’s edges look like, and what the carpet’s do. It only knows what you taught it, so label honestly: the pattern is floor. Teach it that the carpet is a cable and it will refuse to clean the carpet.
src.t.dw1obl: Random bounce is what the first robots did. It works, like looking for your keys by walking around the house. Eventually. Lanes, like mowing a lawn, visit each place once.
src.t.mi94yu: The brush reaches a little beside the robot, so lanes two tiles apart cover everything; three or four leave stripes. And every metre costs battery: the robot must keep enough to walk back to the dock, which is at the far end.
src.t.pj6pod: It looks straight down and reads how far the floor is. Tiles are close. The dark carpet looks a bit further, because it is dark. The stairs are very far, they are not there at all.
src.t.1xs3stm: You set the line: if the reading falls under it, stop. Too low and the robot does not see the stairs and flies. Too high and the dark carpet looks like a hole and it will not go on it. Between the two, there is a good number, and a bruised intern if you pick wrong.
src.t.trkeoq: Where am I, what is around me, what is on the floor, where do I go next. Four questions, one robot. The sheet says the rest. Do not drop it.
src.t.1ftxv0k: The wheels count how far they turned, and the gyro feels the turn. Together they say how far the robot moved. But wheels slip on carpet, so this guess drifts by itself.
src.t.1wlcxfv: A little laser spins on the roof and measures the distance to everything around it, a ring of numbers per turn. It sees walls and chair legs, but not a cable on the floor.
src.t.8bi27k: A cloud of guesses of where the robot might be. Every scan, the guesses that fit the map stay and the others go. The cloud collapses onto the robot.
src.t.nga730: The robot draws its own map: every beam says “air all along here, and something at the end”. Evidence adds up, so one wrong beam cannot ruin a wall and the cat’s ghost fades.
src.t.1qaxxbk: A small camera at the front looks at the floor. The lidar flies over a cable; the camera is what sees it. Someone has to tell it what cables and socks look like first.
src.t.hinaj7: A filter picks out what matters in the picture, and a small network learns clear floor, cable or sock. Too jumpy and it refuses the carpet; too blind and it eats the charger.
src.t.18bvffj: It picks the next tile to clean, finds a way there on the map and steers. Lanes like mowing a lawn cover the floor fastest. When the battery is low it plans the way home.
src.t.1ms48f0: The part that touches the floor. Suction drains the battery, the cliff sensor stops it at the stairs, and the dock’s beacon guides the last metre home.
src.t.1aoihoc: Demo time. Show me Rumbay. And it better not crash.
src.t.1q9w3qu: Rumbay. A robot that cleans the garage by itself, with a map it drew itself.
src.t.u1xp8n: I put my coffee on the floor. It went round it. I put my sock on the floor. It went round that, too. Where is my intern? Never mind.
src.t.1uq8wlz: A robot that knows where it is. More than most of us.
src.t.120h92g: It has been going round and round for an hour and plays a song. A *sad* song. Who taught it sad?
src.t.1u36mg7: The poor thing. It thinks it is in the kitchen. Tea will not fix it, but tea will not hurt.
src.t.dcwhew: Listen up. Photos. Everyone edits photos. *We* send them to a man called Selim who edits them for forty lira. That ends today.
src.t.td778z: It’s called *Fotoşop*. Like the famous one, but I’ve already written the pricing: seven lira a month, per layer, and the undo is a premium feature. Legal says that’s “brave”.
src.t.1r2t5pp: Layers, filters, a slider that shows before and after. The slider is the whole demo. Also: my face on every photo. With the scratch removed. I have a scratch.
src.t.1xidcsu: Tea, anyone? Tip: a photo is not “what it looks like”. It’s numbers, and the numbers need a note saying what they mean. Keep your eye on the *edges*: of layers, of the picture, of the cache.
src.t.ikyx1c: I’ll take the maths of blending. Someone want the blur? It’s the filter everybody’s filter is made of.
src.t.1boaiux: Because the numbers in a photo are not amounts of light. They are squeezed: a file stores 0.5 for a tone that is only a fifth as bright as 1.0, because your eye notices differences in the dark far more than in the bright.
src.t.3n4nf5: Half a lamp on is 0.735 in the file. If you average the *numbers* you get 0.5, which is a quarter of the light. Dark fringes on soft edges, muddy gradients: that is why. Decode to light, blend, encode again.
src.t.a16pc4: *Multiply* is two glasses of tea stacked: the light has to pass through both, so it only ever gets darker. *Screen* is two lamps pointed at one wall: it only ever gets lighter. *Overlay* does multiply to the dark half and screen to the bright half, so contrast goes up.
src.t.grhxgy: Same formulas whatever the space. What changes the look is whether you run them on light or on the stored numbers.
src.t.ef67s4: A blur is each pixel becoming the weighted average of the pixels around it. Done square-style, a radius of 8 means 17 times 17: 289 sums for every pixel.
src.t.1kevyjq: A Gaussian has a trick: blur along the rows, then along the columns, and you get the exact same picture with 17 plus 17 sums. Like serving a whole floor: first every row, then every column, instead of every person against every other.
src.t.92d47t: A pixel that is not there still has a colour in the file: black. Blur the colours alone and that black seeps into the edge.
src.t.63920u: The fix is *premultiplied alpha*: multiply the colour by its opacity first, so see-through counts for nothing, blur, and divide it back out. Like diluting tea with water: you must count how much tea is in the glass, not just how brown it is.
src.t.3ym60p: It has to look at neighbours that do not exist. You must make them up. *Clamp* repeats the last pixel. *Mirror* reflects the picture. *Wrap* takes the opposite side. *Zero* says everything out there is black.
src.t.ewy0s8: Zero gives the picture a dark frame after a blur. Wrap leaks the left edge into the right. Clamp is the quiet one: the last pixel is the best guess for the next.
src.t.1jfdlx8: Blur the photo, subtract the blur from the original, and what is left is the detail. Add some of the detail back. The name is from darkrooms: they used a blurry negative as a mask.
src.t.rrlhhf: Radius is how fat the detail is, amount how much you add, threshold lets you skip tiny differences like grain. Too much amount and the pixels run out of range, burnt to pure black or white, with halos beside every edge.
src.t.umhlaz: Count how many pixels are at each brightness and draw it as bars. A hazy photo is a hill pushed into one corner: the darkest pixel is not black and the brightest not white.
src.t.1qs6jvd: Levels pull the black point and the white point to where the hill starts and ends. Every tone gets stretched to fill the range. Pull too far and the ends are cut off: those pixels are clipped, and detail there is gone for good.
src.t.l16fsl: A file says “0.9, 0.3, 0.1”. Which red? sRGB is the plain screen’s idea. Display P3 is the phone screen’s richer idea. The same numbers mean different colours.
src.t.1tjm3fd: Read a P3 file as sRGB and everything is dull. Read an sRGB file as P3 and it is garish. The profile in the file is the note that tells you which: read it, then convert to what the screen shows.
src.t.1fbzrb8: It does not invent. It looks around the hole, finds a place in the photo whose neighbours look just like the hole’s neighbours, and copies what is there. On a brick wall that finds another brick and mortar joint.
src.t.ao5g46: The lazy version fills one average colour: the scratch is gone and a plaster is left. Ask me how I know.
src.t.1ub0rk4: A 24-megapixel photo is 96 megabytes. Fifty undo steps would be nearly five gigabytes. The machine would sit down and cry.
src.t.11bsuy6: But a brush stroke only changes a few squares of the picture. Cut the photo into tiles, and for each step save only the tiles it touched: about a megabyte. The tiles also let you draw only what is on the screen, and keep the last ones warm in a cache.
src.t.i08n06: JPEG cuts the picture into 8-by-8 squares and writes each as a mix of waves, from broad to fine. Then it rounds the numbers, the fine waves harder, because your eye misses them.
src.t.1394gdl: Quality is how hard it rounds. At about 85 you save most of the size and nobody sees. At 30 you see the squares. At 100 you keep everything, including grain, and the file is huge. PNG keeps all of it, exactly.
src.t.zk94gr: A photo comes in, goes through tone, healing and filters, sits in layers, and goes out. Nine boxes. The rest is pixels.
src.t.1v9vcgm: A photo is a grid of numbers plus a note saying what the numbers mean: the colour profile. Lose the note and the colours drift.
src.t.ex4h7i: Levels stretch a hazy photo so it uses the whole range from black to white. The profile says how to turn the file’s numbers into the screen’s colours.
src.t.vuet9r: The healing brush looks around for a piece of the photo whose surroundings match the hole’s, and copies it in. Bricks stay bricks.
src.t.1kencyl: Filters average each pixel with its neighbours. A Gaussian can be done as a row pass and a column pass, which is much faster. At the photo’s border you must decide what lies beyond.
src.t.12efbgv: Layers are sheets of glass with a picture and an alpha. Each pixel is mixed with what is below it by the blend mode. Do the mixing in light, and a half-lit lamp is half as bright to the eye.
src.t.d9bnt5: A 24-megapixel photo is far too big to redraw as one piece. It is cut into tiles, and only the ones on the screen are decoded; recently used ones stay in a cache.
src.t.qf26q0: Undo has to remember what each step changed. Keeping a whole copy per step is 96 megabytes each; keeping only the tiles the brush touched is about one.
src.t.4zta4a: What you see: the layers blended and converted to the screen’s colours.
src.t.5bs6p0: Export squeezes the picture into a file. JPEG throws away detail the eye misses, in 8-by-8 blocks, and quality says how much to throw away. Too much and the blocks show.
src.t.1t1si3o: Demo time. Show me Fotoşop. And it better not crash.
src.t.10xd2et: The camera’s own IMU: where the lens really points right now. Using only this reacts after the shake has happened: feedback.
src.t.13nzc0n: integrate() adds up the camera’s error over time and pushes against it until it is gone: slow but sure.
src.t.1tl2jq4: KFB is the feedback gain: how fast the gimbal chases what the camera’s own sensor says is wrong.
src.t.sujkyb: The path the drone flies to the tea table. A detour is longer but keeps clear of the boss’s office.
src.t.60a6kx: Cruise speed in metres per second. The faster it goes, the more it has to tilt to speed up and slow down, and the more the tea slops.
src.t.34cud2: Telemetry is the drone’s report back over the radio: attitude, position, battery. More reports a second show fresher data, but fill a radio that only carries so much.
src.t.93migg: A heartbeat is a tiny “I am still here” message the ground station sends five times a second. If none comes for a few seconds, the drone decides the link is dead.
src.t.nvlxbe: What the drone does by itself when it stops hearing the ground station, after the wait in seconds. Return home is the usual safe answer.
src.t.1m0o3ny: The charge at which the drone gives up the mission and goes home or lands. Too late and it does not make it back.
src.t.c3pb0b: A fence in the air: a circle round the boss’s office. When the drone reaches it, it stops and hovers, or goes home.
src.t.1qp0ahs: Maps. Everyone has maps. I have been lost for eleven years and *nobody* has a map for it.
src.t.17pbmz3: It is called *Mapsiz*. It means “without a map”. It is a joke. Legal says it is a joke. Legal is also lost.
src.t.1q57tuf: I type Taksim, I type Kadıköy, I get a line, a time and some turns. And it must know about the *bridge*. Everyone knows about the bridge.
src.t.umxlvk: Tea, anyone? The road file has *roads through the sea*, streets listed twice and a gated estate nobody can reach. Clean first, then draw the graph.
src.t.hboiyk: I will do the search part. People type “Kadikoy” with no dots.
src.t.mvs8bu: Open the 📋 board on a laptop. Roads and place search can start right now; the router waits for the graph.
src.t.hh9vrd: Between two houses in a city there are more routes than there are glasses of tea in Turkey. So you do not try them all. You start at A, always take the nearest unfinished corner and write down how long it took to reach it.
src.t.wg611x: That is Dijkstra: it spreads out like a puddle in every direction at once. A* is the same puddle, but it leans towards B.
src.t.4dfes9: It is the hunch of how long is left. “As the crow flies, at top speed” is a good hunch: no road can beat a crow.
src.t.lkyx9i: The one rule: the guess must *never be more than the truth*. If the hunch is too proud, A* skips the highway because “it surely isn’t worth it”, and hands you a slower way very quickly. Like me taking the stairs because I was sure the lift was broken.
src.t.le4sel: A graph is dots and arrows. A normal street is two arrows, one each way. A one-way street is one arrow.
src.t.19hd7fo: If you draw two arrows for every street, the app sends people the wrong way down it. If you draw one for every street, half the town is a trap you can enter and never leave.
src.t.giqwpk: Two witnesses. History says: “the bridge is always bad at half past eight”. Live phones say: “there was an accident ten minutes ago”. History is calm and a little old; the phones are fresh and a little drunk.

src.t.a40t0s: Also a letter O with a hole, and a star. And you click on the star and it selects the star. I know it is simple. I have asked three agencies.
src.t.ccv09h: Tea, anyone? Tip: nothing in a vector editor is pixels until the very last step. It is all numbers and curves. So *where* you cut corners decides what breaks when somebody zooms in.
src.t.jyfjwp: I’ll take the curves. Someone want the rasteriser? That’s where the pixels come from.
src.t.e95s4y: Four points. The first and last are where the curve begins and ends. The middle two are handles: the curve is pulled towards them but never touches them. Like a rope held at both ends while two friends tug it sideways.
src.t.18hlsfi: To find the point at t, mix each pair of neighbours by t, giving three points. Mix those pairs, giving two. Mix again: one point. It lies on the curve. Moving t from nought to one traces it. That is de Casteljau, and it is all there is.
src.t.1ygcgfo: Because filling a curve directly is hard, and filling a polygon is easy: walk across, count edges. So the editor cuts every curve into tiny straight segments first. This is *flattening*.
src.t.dau0zu: The art is the number of pieces. Few and a circle looks like a stop sign; hundreds and you waste everything. A straight stretch needs one piece; a tight bend needs many. So you cut where it curves.
src.t.o1e91e: Say pieces may stray by a tenth of a unit. At normal size a unit is one pixel and that is invisible. Zoom in sixteen times and the same tenth of a unit is a pixel and a half, a visible kink.
src.t.dtwf3o: So the tolerance is divided by the zoom: when you zoom, the editor cuts again with finer pieces. Zoom independence is not magic, it is re-flattening on every zoom.
src.t.1fxxgyk: Draw two circles the same way round, one inside the other. Which part is painted? *Non-zero*: count how many times the outline winds around the spot. The middle winds twice, so it is painted: no hole. *Even-odd*: count crossings of a ray. The middle has two, an even number: a hole.
src.t.19la1vq: The letter O wants even-odd. The pentagram’s middle is wound twice: non-zero paints it, even-odd leaves a pentagon hole. The shape carries its rule.
src.t.1utor6g: It sends a ray off to the right and counts what it crosses, with the fill rule. A click inside the hole of the O crosses two edges: even-odd says outside. Good: you clicked the table behind it.
src.t.1nkxipo: The lazy way is the box around the shape. Fast, and you can select a star by clicking the empty corner next to it. Customers notice that.
src.t.1nuhj2v: A thick line is a flat ribbon. At a corner the outer edges leave a gap or overlap. *Miter* extends the edges until they meet, in a point. *Round* fills with an arc. *Bevel* cuts the corner off.
src.t.mtsjy6: A very sharp corner mitered gives a spike many times the width, like a pencil stuck out of a glass. The *miter limit* says: if the point would be longer than this, bevel instead.
src.t.11wxitf: A cap is added to every end. A round or square cap sticks out half the width. A dash with a gap of six and a width of six has both neighbours stretching three into it: the gap is gone. Butt caps end exactly where they should.
src.t.terz8i: A pixel is a little square, and an edge goes through it at an angle. One sample at the centre says inside or outside: stairs. Take several samples and count how many are inside: a quarter inside makes it a quarter dark.
src.t.pfwuaz: Costs scale with the number of samples. Four looks nearly like sixteen on most edges. The boss thinks sixteen is four times better. It is four times slower.
src.t.10qya2p: Every coordinate is rounded to the decimals you write. One decimal is fine at normal size and a bit wobbly on a billboard. Two decimals is a hundredth of a unit: invisible even sixteen times larger. Four is a longer file for nothing.
src.t.1oh40m6: Relative coordinates (“move by this much from where you are”) look shorter but every rounding adds to the next, so the shape slowly drifts. Absolute coordinates each round on their own.
src.t.udsino: Curves in the document, segments for the machine, pixels only at the very end. Nine boxes; the pixels are the last one.
src.t.zu3d76: The drawing is not pixels but a list of shapes. Each shape is a few curves, each curve four points. Move one point and only that curve changes.
src.t.16g5s9g: Given four points and a t between nought and one, mix neighbouring points by t, then the mixes, then the mix of those: one point is left, and it is on the curve.
src.t.1h3b9tm: Machines like straight lines. The flattener cuts each curve into short segments, as many as the bend needs, none straying more than a fraction of a pixel.
src.t.zwbx4g: A click shoots a ray and counts what it crosses. The fill rule says how to read the count, so holes are holes and a star can be filled in the middle.
src.t.awws8m: A thick line is a polygon around a thin one. At the corners and the ends you choose the style, and a sharp mitered corner needs a limit, or it spikes.
src.t.1i6rqch: The only place pixels appear. Each pixel gets the share of it the shape covers; one sample gives stairs, several give smooth edges.
src.t.okkqer: What you see. Zoom in and everything is flattened and drawn again at the new scale, so the curves stay curves.
src.t.1m83d4e: The drawing as text. Every control point is written with some number of decimals: too few and the shapes wobble when zoomed in, too many and the file is bloated.
src.t.xevy3x: Demo time. Show me Illüstratör. And it better not crash.
src.t.w7pme0: Illüstratör. Shapes that never get pixels. Zoom in as far as the boss’s ego.
src.t.105lpnx: I zoomed the tea glass until it was bigger than Rıza. Smooth. I have asked the printers to put it on the building. They said “which building”. All of them.
src.t.1mzxztn: The letter O is a filled circle and the star is a bag of triangles. Rıza says it is “abstract”. I say it is a refund.
